description.narrative: The PNG Australia Transition to Health is Australia’s program for delivering technical assistance, projects and grants to PNG's health sector in line with both the Government of Australia and PNG’s outcomes for health in Papua New Guinea. It is envisaged that the investment though the managing contractor will perform four main functions in support of delivering these outcomes: Design and management of sub-programs, provision of high quality technical assistance, provision of high quality policy advice to DFAT and grant management.

description.narrative: Australia is helping to address unmet need for contraception and family planning services in PNG through supporting Marie Stopes PNG to increase availability and utilisation of high-quality contraceptives and family planning services. In 2022, the program delivered both static and mobile outreach clinics that provided integrated sexual and reproductive health services and provided community-based training and targeted communication products to generate awareness and interest in the uptake of the services.

Australia supported extension of the electronic tuberculosis information management system (eTB) to three additional PNG provinces (totalling eight provinces), to strengthen tuberculosis surveillance systems. eTB has registered 15,800 geo-located tuberculosis patients, providing timely electronic records that can be accessed by clinicians, community health workers and provincial health authorities. This enables improved management and treatment of mobile and remote patients. The mapping of tuberculosis cases in PNG allows efficient contact tracing and treatment follow-up, thus reducing infection rates, illness and deaths.

Australia supported piloting of a PNG-led emergency medical response team in June to December 2022. The multidisciplinary teams (consisting of 39 trained participants - 22 women and 17 men) included infection prevention and control specialists, emergency medical clinicians and biomedical technicians. The teams were deployed to four provinces to improve health security threat responses, training a further 87 provincial health staff (45 women; 42 men) to improve infection prevention and control measures, the use of oxygen supplies and biomedical equipment maintenance to reduce health worker exposure to COVID-19 and other infectious diseases.

Australia supports increased childhood immunisation coverage in PNG through the Accelerated Immunisation and Health Systems Strengthening Program (AIHSS), co-funded with New Zealand and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. In 2022, two previously low coverage provinces achieved dramatic increases in immunisation rates. With AIHSS support, the Autonomous Region of Bougainville increased the number of vaccinations given by 121 percent compared to 2021, and West Sepik increased vaccinations by 82 percent. AIHSS was central to this success through funding integrated outreach and mobile services to provided immunisation and other maternal and child health services across the provinces.

In 2024, Australia supported PNG's Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL) to develop its first-ever Strategic Plan (2025-2030). An Australian-funded subject matter expert worked closely with CPHL throughout the process, supporting comprehensive consultations, drafting workshops, and alignment with national health policies. The Strategic Plan provides a clear roadmap for strengthening laboratory systems nationwide and sets the stage for the integration of CPHL with the National Reference Laboratory (NRL) by 2027. It is now before the senior executive management of National Department of Health for endorsement.

In 2024, Australian support helped to improve TB diagnostic capabilities at Port Moresby General Hospital (PMGH). As a result, PMGH recorded the highest number of paediatric TB cases at a single centre in PNG, and worldwide, diagnosing and treating 1,209 children for drug-sensitive tuberculosis (DS-TB). This marks significant progress toward improved TB care for children in PNG and efforts to tackle the country’s TB epidemic. ‍ Expanded access to GeneXpert technology, culture-based diagnostics and improved clinical screening and referral systems at PMGH enabled the high rate of diagnosis. The project also integrated HIV screening into paediatric TB services, with 93% (1,126) of children diagnosed with TB also tested for HIV. ‍ Australian Government funding for the Child TB/HIV Project also supports specialist training in pediatric TB/HIV, staff salaries, and operational costs.

In 2024, Australian support, through the PNG-Australia Transition to Health (PATH) program, for the Morobe Provincial Health Authority (MPHA) to raise its public financial management standards, enabled it to regain access to national funding for the first time since 2017. ‍ Working in partnership with the Provincial Health Authority, the program analysed primary health data and implemented proper budgeting and reporting processes. An evidence-based funding proposal submitted to the Department of Treasury resulted in national government funding being reinstated and helped the MPHA secure a 29% increase in its national funding appropriation for 2025. ‍ Morobe’s success is informing a pilot in 2025 of the same model in the Western Provincial Health Authority.

In the remote North Fly District, Western Province - which has some of the highest rates of tuberculosis (TB) in the world - Australia supported the training of 43 treatment supporters and clinical staff to identify the signs of TB, support patients to commence and complete treatment, and manage medication side effects. The training improved the District's capacity to find people with TB symptoms and improve TB care. The training led to a request from the district for ongoing mentoring which Australia is now supporting through a new TB counsellor program in Kiunga in 2024. This will build long-term cacpacity and improve outcomes.

Support from the Australian Government to the Burnet Institute’s TB Fellowship Program has grown a national centre of excellence, building clinical and leadership capacity for tuberculosis (TB) control. Initially focused on Western Province, the program expanded across Papua New Guinea. By 2024, 10 fellows had graduated. ‍ Ms. Hariet Topa, a Health Extension Officer from New Ireland Province, is the program’s first female fellow. Upon completing the12-month program she was appointed Coordinator of the New Ireland Provincial TB Program, where she now leads efforts to implement local TB elimination strategies. The fellowship program fosters sustainable, province-led TB responses, gender-inclusive leadership, and national collaboration.

The Australian Government’s Partnering for Strong Families (PSF) Project is supporting PNG to increase access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services and rights. Health workers such as Gaudi, an experienced SRH nurse employed by Marie Stopes and funded by Australia, played a key role in increasing Couple-Years of Protection (CYP) in Lae (Morobe Province) almost five-fold from 6,011 in 2023 to 29,318 in 2024. These results were achieved by addressing gaps among key populations, including counselling for postnatal mothers on the family planning options available. Most mothers prefer longer-term methods and there is growing demand for IUDs. Community outreach teams focused on reaching adolescents, addressing stigma, cost, and distance barriers. Using humour and peer engagement approaches created safe, welcoming spaces for youth to access SRH services.

The Trilateral Malaria Project improved diagnosis and real-time surveillance of malaria at the PNG’s Central Public Health Laboratory through the purchase of reagents and laboratory consumable equipment which has assisted the newly appointed Malaria PCR Scientist to establish rapid diagnostic Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) testing for malaria. This has widened the range of malaria species able to be detected and improved the accuracy of diagnosis of malaria in PNG.

Through the PNG Australia Transition to Health (PATH), DFAT's support this reporting period has generated 71,262 Couple-Years of Protection (CYP), the estimated protection from pregnancy provided by contraceptive methods over a one year period. The Partnering for Strong Families project includes dedicated family planning nurses embedded in hospitals, raising awareness among hospital staff and patients of the critical role family planning plays in reducing maternal and infant mortality and preventing unwanted pregnancies. There has been an observed uptake of family planning services, particularly long-acting reversible contraceptive methods; secured the availability of family planning commodities in hospital pharmacies, and an increase in the range and number of qualified medical officers capable of providing family planning services. In 2023, 5,926 individuals accessed family planning and/or sexual and reproductive health services provided by the embedded nurses.

With support from the PNG-Australia Transition to Health program, the Southern Highlands Provincial Health Authority (SHPHA) improved its public financial management compliance score from 60% in January 2024 to 90% by September 2024. This was achieved through standardised budgeting tools, more detailed audits, tighter procurement oversight, and regular Corrective Action Plan reviews. As a result of this support, SHPHA senior management reported increased confidence and capacity to effectively carry out their core responsibilities. These efforts enabled SHPHA to qualify for an independent transition review and. for the first time in five years, gained approval to directly manage an immunisation program grant funded by Australia, New Zealand and Gavi.
